If you manage it yourself, you typically run it on a regular cadence after compaction, often with a DRY RUN first to see what would be removed. The trend is to let the platform handle it so storage cleanup happens reliably without manual cron jobs.

question: What practical levers do you have to reduce DBU usage and overall Databricks cost?
directAnswer: Cost on Databricks is DBUs times the rate times time, so you pull levers on all three. On rate and lifecycle: run scheduled work on job clusters at the lower Jobs rate, reserve all-purpose clusters for development with short auto-termination, and use spot instances with on-demand fallback for fault-tolerant workers. On time: enable Photon and AQE to finish jobs faster, fix shuffles and skew so jobs stop wasting compute, and keep tables compacted and clustered so queries read less data. On capacity: use autoscaling with sensible bounds so you pay for peaks only when needed, and right-size warehouses by separating per-query size from concurrency. Finally, you measure: use system tables and tags to attribute spend, find the most expensive jobs, and target tuning where the money actually goes rather than guessing.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Reducing DBU usage is the practice of lowering the billable Databricks Units a workload consumes, through a mix of cheaper compute choices, faster execution, elastic capacity, and good table maintenance, guided by measurement of where spend concentrates.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Databricks bills by DBUs consumed over time, and without deliberate management costs balloon from idle clusters, the wrong pricing tier, slow jobs, and over-provisioning. The discipline exists because the cheapest DBU is the one you never spend, and most platforms have substantial waste that targeted changes can remove.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks:
You combine compute, performance, and measurement levers and prioritize by where the money is.

```sql
-- Find the costliest jobs to target first (system tables)
SELECT usage_metadata.job_id, SUM(usage_quantity) AS dbus
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_date >= current_date() - 30
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY dbus DESC LIMIT 20;
```

Then apply: job clusters and spot for cheaper compute, Photon/AQE and shuffle/skew fixes for shorter runtime, autoscaling and right-sized warehouses for elastic capacity, and OPTIMIZE/VACUUM (or Predictive Optimization) so queries scan less and storage stays lean. The measurement step ensures you tune the few jobs that dominate the bill instead of micro-optimizing cheap ones.

whyImportant: Cost optimization is a core senior-engineer responsibility on Databricks, and interviewers want a structured, measurement-driven answer rather than a single trick. Showing you think in terms of rate, time, and capacity, and that you target spend with data, signals you can actually lower a platform's bill responsibly.
realWorldExample: A platform's bill was dominated, on inspection of system.billing.usage, by a handful of jobs running on always-on all-purpose clusters. Moving those to job clusters on spot with fallback, enabling Photon so they finished faster, and right-sizing the BI warehouse to Serverless with auto-stop together cut the monthly spend significantly, and crucially the team knew which changes mattered because they started from the cost data, not guesses.

nestedTopics.title: Rate and lifecycle levers
nestedTopics.explanation: Choosing the cheaper Jobs Compute rate for scheduled work, terminating idle all-purpose clusters, and using spot instances for recoverable workers all lower what you pay per unit of compute and eliminate idle waste. These are often the largest and easiest savings because they fix structural choices rather than squeezing individual queries.

nestedTopics.title: Runtime and efficiency levers
nestedTopics.explanation: Anything that makes a job finish sooner reduces DBUs consumed: Photon and AQE, eliminating unnecessary shuffles, fixing skew, pruning columns, and keeping tables compacted and clustered so queries scan less data. Faster jobs are cheaper jobs, so performance tuning and cost tuning are largely the same activity here.

nestedTopics.title: Measure before optimizing
nestedTopics.explanation: System tables and cluster/job tags let you attribute spend to specific jobs, teams, and clusters, so you can rank where the money goes and optimize the top items first. Without measurement you risk polishing cheap jobs while expensive ones run unexamined, so the measurement step is what makes the rest efficient.

followUps.question: What is the single biggest source of waste you usually find?
followUps.answer: Idle and mis-tiered compute: production jobs running on always-on all-purpose clusters, and development clusters left running with no auto-termination. These pay both the higher rate and for idle hours, and they are common because they accrete quietly. Fixing them by moving scheduled work to job clusters and enforcing auto-termination often yields the biggest, fastest savings before any query-level tuning.

followUps.question: How do tags help with cost management?
followUps.answer: Custom tags on clusters, jobs, and warehouses propagate into the billing data, letting you group spend by team, project, environment, or cost center. That makes it possible to attribute and charge back costs, spot which team or pipeline is driving spend, and set budgets. Without tags the bill is one undifferentiated number; with them you can hold owners accountable and target the right workloads.

followUps.question: Is making a job faster always the same as making it cheaper?
followUps.answer: Usually but not always. Faster typically means fewer DBU-seconds, so cheaper, but if you achieve speed by using a much larger or higher-rate cluster, the per-hour cost can rise enough to offset the shorter runtime. The honest framing is total cost equals rate times time, so you check both: a change that halves runtime on the same cluster is a clear win, while one that doubles cluster size for a small speedup may not be.

question: How do you tune Structured Streaming on Databricks, including trigger and maxFilesPerTrigger?
directAnswer: Streaming tuning is about balancing latency, throughput, and cost, and the main levers are the trigger and the per-batch input limits. The trigger controls how often a micro-batch runs: a processing-time trigger runs continuously for low latency, while AvailableNow processes all available data in batches then stops, which is ideal for cost-efficient incremental batch jobs that do not need a cluster running all day. The input-rate limits, maxFilesPerTrigger for file sources and maxOffsetsPerTrigger for Kafka, cap how much data each micro-batch ingests, which keeps batches a manageable size so they do not overwhelm memory or create huge uneven batches when catching up after a backlog. You tune these by watching batch duration and backlog in the streaming metrics: if batches take longer than the trigger interval you are falling behind, so you either raise resources or lower the per-batch limit to keep batches stable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Structured Streaming tuning is configuring how a continuous query consumes and processes data in micro-batches. The trigger sets batch cadence; maxFilesPerTrigger and maxOffsetsPerTrigger cap input per batch; and supporting choices like state store and checkpointing affect stability and cost.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A streaming query that ingests unbounded data must control batch size and frequency, or it will create batches too large to fit in memory (especially when catching up on a backlog) or run too frequently to be efficient. These knobs exist to keep micro-batches stable and right-sized, and to let you trade latency for cost depending on whether the workload is truly real-time or incremental-batch.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks:
You pick a trigger and per-batch limits to match the latency requirement and keep batches steady.

```python
(spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles")
   .option("cloudFiles.format", "json")
   .option("cloudFiles.maxFilesPerTrigger", 1000)  # cap files per batch
   .load(src)
 .writeStream
   .trigger(availableNow=True)   # process backlog in batches, then stop
   # .trigger(processingTime="1 minute")  # continuous low-latency option
   .option("checkpointLocation", ckpt)
   .toTable("bronze_events"))
```

For latency-sensitive work use a short processing-time trigger; for cost-efficient incremental loads use AvailableNow so a job cluster runs, drains the backlog in bounded batches, and terminates. You set maxFilesPerTrigger/maxOffsetsPerTrigger so each batch is large enough to be efficient but small enough to stay within memory and finish within the interval.

whyImportant: Streaming is where misconfiguration most easily causes instability and runaway cost, so interviewers probe whether you understand triggers, per-batch limits, and the latency-versus-cost trade-off, including the AvailableNow pattern that turns streaming into cheap incremental batch. It shows you can run streaming pipelines that are stable and economical, not just functional.
realWorldExample: An ingestion stream with no maxFilesPerTrigger fell behind during an upstream backfill, then tried to process a million files in one giant batch, ran out of memory, and crashed. Setting maxFilesPerTrigger to a bounded value made it drain the backlog in steady, memory-safe batches, and switching the job to an AvailableNow trigger let it run on a job cluster a few times a day, process everything available, and terminate, cutting cost versus an always-on stream.

nestedTopics.title: Choosing a trigger
nestedTopics.explanation: A processing-time trigger runs micro-batches on a fixed interval for continuous low-latency streaming, keeping a cluster running. AvailableNow processes all currently available data in bounded batches and then stops, which suits incremental loads that can run periodically on a job cluster and terminate, trading latency for much lower cost. The choice follows whether the workload truly needs real-time freshness.

nestedTopics.title: Per-batch input limits
nestedTopics.explanation: maxFilesPerTrigger (file/Auto Loader sources) and maxOffsetsPerTrigger (Kafka) cap how much each micro-batch ingests, which keeps batch sizes bounded and predictable. Without them, a backlog produces one massive batch that can exhaust memory. With them, the stream catches up in steady increments, so the limits are essential for stability under bursty or delayed input.

nestedTopics.title: Reading streaming metrics
nestedTopics.explanation: The streaming query metrics show batch duration, input rows per batch, and processing rate versus input rate. If batch duration exceeds the trigger interval or backlog grows, the stream is falling behind and you must add resources or lower per-batch limits. These metrics are the streaming equivalent of the Spark UI for tuning decisions.

followUps.question: When would you choose AvailableNow over a continuous trigger?
followUps.answer: When the data does not need to be processed in seconds and you want to avoid paying for an always-on cluster. AvailableNow lets a scheduled job cluster spin up, process all available data in bounded micro-batches with full streaming semantics like exactly-once and checkpointing, then shut down, so you get incremental processing at batch cost. Continuous triggers are for genuinely latency-sensitive use cases where freshness justifies a running cluster.

followUps.question: What happens if you set maxFilesPerTrigger too low or too high?
followUps.answer: Too low means many tiny batches, each with fixed per-batch overhead, so throughput drops and the stream may never catch up on a backlog. Too high means batches that can exceed memory and cause spill or failures, and uneven, long batches. You tune it from the metrics: pick a value where each batch finishes comfortably within the interval and stays within memory, which keeps the stream both stable and efficient.

followUps.question: How does checkpointing affect streaming tuning and reliability?
followUps.answer: The checkpoint stores offsets and state so the query can recover exactly-once after a restart, so a stable, dedicated checkpoint location is essential and you never share one across queries. For stateful operations, the state store size grows with keys, so tuning includes bounding state with watermarks to drop old state and avoid unbounded growth. Good checkpointing and watermark configuration are what keep a long-running stream both correct and from slowly degrading over time.

question: What are deletion vectors, and how do they speed up updates and deletes on Delta?
directAnswer: Deletion vectors are a merge-on-read optimization for Delta that lets a DELETE, UPDATE, or MERGE mark specific rows as removed without rewriting the whole data files that contain them. Normally Delta is copy-on-write: deleting even one row from a file forces rewriting that entire file, which is expensive when files are large and only a few rows change. With deletion vectors enabled, Delta instead writes a small side file recording which row positions in a data file are deleted, and readers skip those rows on the fly. This makes deletes and updates dramatically faster and cheaper for selective changes, at the cost of a little read-time work to apply the vectors, which is later cleaned up when OPTIMIZE physically rewrites the files. It is a key reason MERGE-heavy and CDC workloads run much faster on modern Delta.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Deletion vectors are compact structures that record which rows in a Parquet data file are logically deleted, so the file itself does not need to be rewritten when rows are removed or updated. They turn Delta's row-level changes from copy-on-write into a merge-on-read approach for the deleted rows.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: In copy-on-write, changing a single row means rewriting its entire data file, so a small DELETE or UPDATE touching rows scattered across many large files can rewrite enormous amounts of data, dominating the cost of selective changes and CDC. Deletion vectors exist to avoid that write amplification by recording deletions cheaply and deferring the physical rewrite until a maintenance step.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks:
On a delete or update, Delta writes a deletion vector marking the affected row positions instead of rewriting the file; reads consult the vector and skip those rows, and updates write the new row versions as new data.

```sql
-- Enable deletion vectors on a table
ALTER TABLE customers
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true');

-- Selective deletes/updates now avoid full-file rewrites
DELETE FROM customers WHERE status = 'closed';
```

The deferred cost is small read-time work to apply vectors and accumulating marked-but-not-removed rows; running OPTIMIZE later physically rewrites files to purge the deleted rows and consolidate, restoring clean files.

whyImportant: Deletion vectors are a major modern Delta performance feature for update- and delete-heavy workloads like CDC and GDPR deletes, and interviewers want to see you understand the copy-on-write versus merge-on-read trade-off and that the deferred cost is reclaimed by OPTIMIZE. It shows you grasp how Delta has evolved to make row-level mutations cheap.
realWorldExample: A CDC pipeline applied frequent small MERGEs into large fact files, and each merge rewrote many full files just to change a handful of rows, making the job slow and expensive. Enabling deletion vectors let the merges mark changed rows cheaply instead of rewriting whole files, cutting the merge time substantially, and a periodic OPTIMIZE later purged the marked rows and kept the files clean.

nestedTopics.title: Copy-on-write versus merge-on-read
nestedTopics.explanation: Copy-on-write rewrites whole files on any change, giving clean files but high write cost for small edits. Merge-on-read, which deletion vectors enable for deletes, records changes separately and applies them at read time, giving cheap writes at a small read cost. Deletion vectors let Delta use the cheaper approach for row removals while keeping data files intact.

nestedTopics.title: Read-time application of vectors
nestedTopics.explanation: When reading a file that has a deletion vector, Delta filters out the marked row positions on the fly so deleted rows never appear in results. This adds a little read overhead, but it is far cheaper than the write amplification it avoids, and the overhead shrinks once OPTIMIZE physically removes the deleted rows.

nestedTopics.title: Cleanup via OPTIMIZE
nestedTopics.explanation: Deletion vectors accumulate as marked-deleted rows that still sit in the data files, so over time read overhead grows and space is held. Running OPTIMIZE rewrites the files to physically drop the deleted rows and clear the vectors, consolidating the table. So deletion vectors defer rather than eliminate the rewrite, and maintenance reclaims the deferred cost.

followUps.question: What is the trade-off of enabling deletion vectors?
followUps.answer: You trade cheaper, faster deletes and updates for a small amount of read-time work to apply the vectors and for deleted rows lingering in files until OPTIMIZE rewrites them. For workloads with frequent selective deletes or updates the write savings vastly outweigh the read cost, which is why it is recommended there. For a table that is rarely mutated, the benefit is small, so it matters most for MERGE- and CDC-heavy tables.

followUps.question: Why are deletion vectors especially useful for compliance deletes?
followUps.answer: Requirements like GDPR right-to-be-forgotten mean deleting specific users' rows that are scattered across many large files. Under copy-on-write that rewrites huge amounts of data for a few rows. Deletion vectors mark those rows immediately and cheaply, so the data is logically removed fast, and a later OPTIMIZE physically purges it. This makes frequent, selective compliance deletes practical without rewriting the whole table each time.

followUps.question: Do all readers and engines support deletion vectors?
followUps.answer: Readers must understand the deletion-vector protocol to correctly skip the marked rows; Databricks runtimes do, but older Delta readers or external engines that do not support the feature could read stale or incorrect rows. So before enabling it you confirm all consumers of the table support deletion vectors, since enabling a newer Delta protocol feature can affect compatibility with tools reading the table directly.

question: How do you monitor and attribute Databricks cost and performance using system tables?
directAnswer: System tables are Databricks-managed tables in the system catalog that record operational data like billing usage, compute events, job runs, and query history, so you can analyze cost and performance with plain SQL instead of scraping the UI. For cost, system.billing.usage gives DBU consumption per workload over time, which you join with pricing and group by job, cluster, or tags to see exactly where money goes and rank the most expensive workloads. For performance, query history and job run tables let you find slow or failing jobs and queries. The workflow is to query these tables to identify the top cost and performance offenders, attribute them to owners using tags, and then target tuning there, and often to build dashboards or alerts on top so cost and reliability are monitored continuously rather than discovered in a surprise bill.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: System tables are read-only, Databricks-maintained tables under the system catalog in Unity Catalog that expose platform telemetry: billing usage, list pricing, compute/cluster events, job and pipeline runs, and query history. They make cost and operational data queryable with SQL and joinable with your own metadata.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Clicking through the UI to understand cost and performance does not scale across many jobs, teams, and clusters, and the billing console alone does not let you attribute spend to specific workloads. System tables exist to give a programmatic, queryable, historical record so you can analyze, attribute, alert on, and chargeback cost and performance with standard tooling.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks:
You query the tables, join usage to pricing, and group by identifiers and tags to attribute and rank spend, then build dashboards or alerts.

```sql
-- Cost by job over the last 30 days, in dollars
SELECT u.usage_metadata.job_id,
       SUM(u.usage_quantity * p.pricing.default) AS est_cost
FROM system.billing.usage u
JOIN system.billing.list_prices p
  ON u.sku_name = p.sku_name
 WHERE u.usage_date >= current_date() - 30
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY est_cost DESC;
```

For performance you query query history and job-run tables to find slow, failing, or queuing workloads. Tags propagated into usage let you group by team or project, and you typically wrap these queries in dashboards and alerts so problems surface continuously.

whyImportant: Modern Databricks cost and reliability management is data-driven, and interviewers want to see you know system tables exist and how to use them to attribute spend and find offenders, rather than relying on the UI or guesswork. It signals you can run governance, chargeback, and continuous monitoring like a platform owner, not just optimize one job at a time.
realWorldExample: Facing an unexplained cost spike, a team queried system.billing.usage joined to list_prices and grouped by tag, and within minutes saw a single mistagged ad-hoc cluster running oversized all-purpose compute around the clock was responsible. They fixed that cluster and then built a scheduled dashboard and alert on the same query so future spikes would be flagged automatically instead of showing up in the next invoice.

nestedTopics.title: Billing usage and pricing tables
nestedTopics.explanation: system.billing.usage records DBU quantities per workload, SKU, and time, and system.billing.list_prices gives the rates, so joining them yields estimated cost. Grouping by job, cluster, SKU, or tag turns raw usage into an attributed cost breakdown you can rank, which is the foundation of cost analysis.

nestedTopics.title: Query history and job run tables
nestedTopics.explanation: System tables for query history and job/pipeline runs expose durations, statuses, and resource use, letting you find the slowest queries, frequently failing jobs, or warehouses with heavy queuing. This is how you locate performance problems across the whole platform with SQL rather than inspecting each job's UI individually.

nestedTopics.title: Tags for attribution
nestedTopics.explanation: Custom tags on clusters, jobs, and warehouses flow into the usage data, so grouping by tag attributes spend to teams, projects, or environments. This enables chargeback, budget tracking, and accountability. Without consistent tagging the cost data is hard to allocate, so a tagging policy is a prerequisite for meaningful attribution.

followUps.question: How would you set up ongoing cost monitoring rather than one-off queries?
followUps.answer: You wrap the system-table cost queries in a Databricks SQL dashboard refreshed on a schedule, and add alerts that trigger when daily DBU spend or a specific job's cost crosses a threshold. That turns cost from something discovered in the monthly bill into something monitored continuously, so anomalies like a runaway cluster are caught within a day. The same pattern works for performance, alerting on job failures or rising query durations.

followUps.question: What is the relationship between system tables and tagging strategy?
followUps.answer: System tables only attribute cost as well as your tags allow, since usage rows carry whatever tags were on the compute. So a consistent, enforced tagging strategy, by team, project, and environment, is what makes the billing tables useful for chargeback and accountability. Investing in tagging policy upfront is what unlocks the analytical value of the cost system tables later.

followUps.question: Can system tables help with performance tuning, not just cost?
followUps.answer: Yes. Query history tables surface the slowest and most resource-hungry queries and warehouses that queue, and job-run tables reveal jobs whose runtimes are creeping up or that fail often. Combined with cost data, you can prioritize tuning the jobs that are both expensive and slow, which is the highest-leverage place to spend engineering effort. So system tables tie performance and cost analysis into one queryable source.
